title: How trading offers work
summary: Who pays in a trading offer, which products you may promote and which to avoid, and how CPA, RevShare and hybrid deals turn qualified depositors into payouts. You finish able to read an offer, calculate effective payout after KYC and qualification, and plan a test with exact starting rules.

lessons.title: The trading affiliate ecosystem
objectives: By the end you can name every player in a trading offer and say what each one wants.
You can explain the four main ways brokers and exchanges earn, and the conflict of interest in one of them.
You can estimate what a client may be worth to a broker and why that sets your payout.
You can plan the cash you need to cover spend while payouts are on hold.

steps.h: Why you must know who pays and why
steps.p: Trading offers often carry some of the larger payouts in affiliate marketing because a funded, active trader can be worth a lot to a broker over time. If you do not understand how the broker earns, you cannot judge an offer, spot a bad one or explain the risk honestly to the people you send.

d.b: A payout is a share of a client's future value
d.s: Understand the value and you understand the offer.

steps.say: Here's why this lesson matters. Trading offers often carry some of the larger payouts in affiliate marketing, because a funded, active trader can be worth a lot to a broker over time. So a payout is really a share of a client's future value. If you don't understand how the broker earns, you can't judge an offer, spot a bad one, or explain the risk honestly to the people you send.

steps.h: Who sits in a trading offer
steps.p: Follow one person from your ad to your payout. Each box is a different business with its own goals and its own rules. Money flows back along the same path, and every box takes a share or applies a check before it reaches you.

Each box is a different business, with its own goals and rules. Money flows back along the same path, and every box takes a share or applies a check before it reaches you.

steps.h: The players and what each one wants
steps.p: Each player has a different job and a different reason to work with you. Knowing what they want tells you what to ask for, what proof to expect and where problems usually start when a deal goes wrong.
steps.more: Introducing brokers are treated differently from simple affiliates in some countries, because they are paid on trading activity and may be seen as arranging deals in investments. Whether you need a registration depends on the country and on what you actually do. We are not certain of the rules in every geo; if you take a per-lot deal, ask the broker and a local adviser whether any registration applies to you.

steps.h: How brokers and exchanges earn
steps.p: Almost all broker revenue comes from the client, either as a cost on each trade or, at some brokers, from client losses. That is why payouts depend on how long and how actively people trade, not on how many sign up.
steps.more: Market making, often called B-book, means the broker does not pass the trade to the wider market but takes the opposite side itself. When the client loses, the broker gains. Many brokers mix models and hedge some trades, and you cannot tell from outside which mix a broker uses. This creates a conflict of interest that regulators know about, and it is one reason risk warnings exist. It matters to you because a RevShare deal on net revenue can include client losses, which we cover in lesson 3.

rows: Gap between buy and sell price
Fixed fee per trade or lot
Fee for holding leveraged trades overnight

steps.say: Here's how brokers and exchanges earn. Look at the table. The spread, the gap between buy and sell price, paid by the client on every trade. Commission, a fixed fee per trade or lot. Overnight financing, for holding leveraged trades overnight. Exchange fees on crypto trades. And market making, where the broker takes the other side of trades, so it earns from client losses. That last one is a conflict of interest regulators know about, and it's one reason risk warnings exist. Almost all broker revenue comes from the client, which is why payouts depend on how long and how actively people trade, not how many sign up.

steps.h: Worked example: what one client may be worth
steps.p: Example. A broker earns about $8 of spread per lot from a client who trades 4 lots a month and stays active for 6 months. That client is worth about $192 in revenue. The broker pays you a share of that, after its own costs.
steps.more: Example maths: 4 × $8 = $32 a month. $32 × 6 = $192. The $8 per lot and the 6 months are illustrative; real figures depend on the instrument, account type and the person. Many clients deposit once and stop within weeks, while a few trade for years. The broker averages across all of them, keeps money for its own costs, compliance and profit, and offers you a payout that still leaves it ahead. That is why brokers add qualification rules: they only want to pay for clients who look like the ones who stay.

steps.h: Worked example: the cash you need while you wait
steps.p: Example. You spend $50 a day through March. The network pays March's approved conversions about 45 days after you started spending. You must fund roughly $2,250 of spend from your own cash before the first payout lands.
steps.more: Many beginners plan their test budget but forget the wait. Spend happens daily on your card. Payouts arrive after a qualification window, a review hold and the payment term, which can add up to several weeks. If you scale during that wait, the gap grows. Plan the cash for spend plus the wait, and never use money you need for rent, food or debts. Trading offers are not a way to get rich quickly, and results vary widely.

steps.h: Why the product decides everything
steps.p: Two offers can pay the same and look alike on a network page, yet one is a licensed broker product and the other is banned from the ad platforms you use. The product decides the regulator, the risk warning, the platform policy and whether you may advertise at all.

steps.h: Worked example: what leverage does
steps.p: Example. A user deposits $200 and trades with leverage of 1:100. They now control a position worth $20,000. A price move of just 1% against them is $200, which is the whole deposit. Leverage multiplies gains and losses alike.
steps.more: Example maths: $200 × 100 = $20,000. 1% of $20,000 = $200. In practice the broker usually closes the position before the balance goes below zero, which is called a stop out. In the UK and EU, retail CFD clients get negative balance protection and leverage is capped, for example at 30:1 on major currency pairs at the time of writing. Many offshore entities offer far higher leverage. That is a risk you should never sell as a feature.

steps.h: Binary and digital options: we do not teach them
steps.p: A binary or digital option asks the user to guess whether a price will be above or below a level after a fixed time, often seconds or minutes. Right, and they get a fixed payout. Wrong, and they lose the whole stake. Major ad platforms prohibit them and many countries ban or restrict them at the time of writing.

d.b: No binary options in this school
d.s: Prohibited on major ad platforms and banned for retail in many countries.

steps.h: How to spot a binary option with a new name
steps.p: Sellers rename the product to get past filters. Judge it by how it works, not by what it is called. If an offer shows several of these signs, treat it as a binary or digital option and steer away, whatever the network calls it.
d: Fixed time|Trade closes itself after 30 seconds, 1 or 5 minutes
Fixed payout|Shown as 'earn 85% if right'
All or nothing|Wrong guess loses 100% of the stake
New names|Digital, turbo, fixed-time, up or down, high or low
Game feel|$1 trades, big green and red buttons, streaks
Licence gap|No retail licence from a major regulator
steps.say: Sellers rename the product to get past filters, so judge it by how it works, not what it's called. Look for these signs. A fixed time, where the trade closes itself after thirty seconds, one or five minutes. A fixed payout, shown as earn eighty five percent if right. All or nothing, where a wrong guess loses the whole stake. New names, like digital, turbo, fixed time, up or down. A game feel, with one dollar trades and big green and red buttons. And a licence gap, with no retail licence from a major regulator. If an offer shows several of these, treat it as a binary option and steer away.

steps.h: Worked example: why the maths works against the user
steps.p: Example. A product pays 85% on a correct guess and takes 100% on a wrong one. A user who is right half the time over 100 trades of $10 wins $425 and loses $500. They end $75 down, before any mistakes.
steps.more: Example maths: 50 wins × $8.50 = $425. 50 losses × $10 = $500. $425 − $500 = −$75. To break even the user must be right more often than 1 ÷ (1 + 0.85), which is about 54.1% of the time, on price moves over seconds or minutes that are close to random. This is why regulators compare these products to gambling and why we do not promote them. If your network offers them, choose a licensed forex, CFD or exchange offer instead.
d: 50 × $10 lost
steps.say: Here's why the maths works against the user. Example: a product pays eighty five percent on a correct guess and takes everything on a wrong one. Over a hundred trades of ten dollars, a user who's right half the time wins four hundred and twenty five dollars and loses five hundred. They end seventy five dollars down, before any mistakes. To break even, they'd need to be right about fifty four percent of the time, on price moves that are close to random. That's why regulators compare these products to gambling, and why we don't promote them.

lessons.title: Payout models: CPA, RevShare and hybrid
objectives: By the end you can compare CPA, RevShare, hybrid and per-lot deals on the same cohort of users.
You can explain negative carryover and calculate a month's payout with it.
You can turn an expected RevShare value into a planning value and a target CPA.
You can list the written terms to confirm before accepting any deal.

steps.h: Why the model matters as much as the number
steps.p: The payout model decides when you are paid, how much risk you carry and what happens when a client wins. Two deals can pay the same total over a year while one leaves you short of cash for months. Choose the model your cash flow can survive.

d.s: The model decides your cash flow.

steps.say: Here's why the model matters as much as the number. The payout model decides when you're paid, how much risk you carry, and what happens when a client wins. Two deals can pay the same total over a year, while one leaves you short of cash for months. Same total, different risk. So choose the model your cash flow can survive.

steps.h: The models you will see
steps.p: Most trading deals are one of these or a mix. Names vary by network, so read the definitions in your agreement rather than trusting the label on the offer page.
d: CPA|Fixed fee per qualified FTD, paid after a hold
RevShare|A percentage of the net revenue your users generate
Hybrid|A smaller CPA plus a smaller RevShare
Per-lot rebate|A fixed amount per lot your users trade
CPL or CPR|Per registration. Rare and low in trading
Volume tiers|Payout steps up with monthly FTDs
steps.say: Here are the models you'll see. C P A, cost per acquisition: a fixed fee per qualified F T D, first time deposit, paid after a hold. RevShare: a percentage of the net revenue your users generate. Hybrid: a smaller C P A plus a smaller RevShare. Per lot rebate: a fixed amount per lot your users trade. C P L or C P R, per registration, which is rare and low in trading. And volume tiers, where the payout steps up with monthly F T Ds. Names vary, so read the definitions in your agreement, not the label.

steps.h: Worked example: one cohort, three models
steps.p: Example. You send 20 FTDs. Over 12 months they generate $3,000 of net revenue for the broker. Compare what you receive under three deals. The totals match on purpose, so you can see that timing and risk are what differ.
steps.more: Example maths: CPA 20 × $60 = $1,200. RevShare 40% × $3,000 = $1,200. Hybrid 20 × $30 = $600 plus 20% × $3,000 = $600, total $1,200. In real life the totals will not match. RevShare can pay far more than CPA if your users trade for years, or far less if they leave quickly or win. CPA moves the risk to the broker and gives you cash sooner. All figures are illustrative.
steps.say: Here's one cohort under three models. Example: you send twenty F T Ds, and over twelve months they generate three thousand dollars of net revenue for the broker. Under C P A at sixty dollars, you get twelve hundred, in month two. Under forty percent RevShare, twelve hundred, spread over twelve months. Under hybrid, thirty dollars each plus twenty percent, also twelve hundred, half early and half spread. The totals match on purpose, so you can see that timing and risk are what differ. In real life they won't match, and all figures are illustrative.

steps.h: Example: RevShare comes from a few users
steps.p: Example. Revenue in a cohort is rarely even. Here 14 of the 20 users produce little, 5 produce a fair amount and 1 produces more than the 14 smallest together. RevShare totals swing heavily with one or two people.
steps.more: Example maths: $280 + $1,000 + $1,720 = $3,000. If the large user had not joined, the cohort would have produced $1,280, and 40% RevShare would pay $512 instead of $1,200. That is why RevShare results from small cohorts are unreliable. Judge RevShare on many cohorts over many months, never on one good month.
d: 14 small users
5 mid users
1 large user
steps.say: Here's an example of where RevShare actually comes from. Revenue in a cohort is rarely even. Look at the bars. Fourteen small users produce two hundred and eighty dollars. Five mid users produce a thousand. And one large user produces seventeen hundred and twenty, more than the fourteen smallest together. If that one user hadn't joined, forty percent RevShare would pay five hundred and twelve dollars instead of twelve hundred. That's why RevShare from small cohorts is unreliable. Judge it on many cohorts over many months.

steps.h: Example: cash received over time
steps.p: Example. You spent $900 on the cohort in month 1. Under CPA you receive $1,200 in month 2 after the hold. Under RevShare the money arrives month by month and has not passed your spend until month 5.
steps.more: Example: RevShare monthly payments of $300, $220, $170, $130, $100, $80 and $30 add up to $1,030 by month 7, with the remaining $170 of the $1,200 arriving over months 8 to 12. The $900 spend is covered in month 5, when the total reaches $920. Under CPA it is covered in month 2. If you keep buying traffic every month on RevShare, these delays stack, and you need much more cash before the deal pays for itself.
steps.say: This chart shows an example of cash received over time. You spent nine hundred dollars on the cohort in month one. Look at the C P A line. You receive twelve hundred in month two, after the hold. Now the RevShare line. Money arrives month by month, three hundred, then two twenty, then less each month, and it doesn't pass your spend until month five. If you keep buying traffic every month on RevShare, these delays stack, and you need much more cash before the deal pays for itself.

steps.h: Worked example: negative carryover
steps.p: Example. Many RevShare deals carry negative months forward. In month 2 your users win $1,500 net, so you earn nothing and start month 3 at minus $1,500. Month 3 earns $1,000, which only shrinks the hole.
steps.more: Example maths: month 3 balance −$1,500 + $1,000 = −$500, so you are paid $0. Month 4 earns $1,200 net: −$500 + $1,200 = $700, and 40% of $700 = $280 is paid. Without carryover you would have been paid 40% × $1,000 = $400 in month 3 and 40% × $1,200 = $480 in month 4. Ask whether the deal has carryover, whether it resets monthly or never, and whether it is per brand or across your whole account. Terms vary; read your agreement.
d: −$1,500 carried
$1,000 in month 3
steps.say: Here's how negative carryover works. Many RevShare deals carry negative months forward. Example: in month two your users win fifteen hundred dollars net, so you earn nothing, and you start month three at minus fifteen hundred. Month three earns a thousand, which only shrinks the hole to minus five hundred, so you're paid zero. Without carryover, you'd have been paid in both months. So ask whether the deal has carryover, whether it resets monthly or never, and whether it's per brand or across your whole account. Terms vary, so read your agreement.

steps.h: The conflict inside net revenue
steps.p: At a market-making broker, net revenue can include client losses. On RevShare you then earn more when your users lose. Never let that change how you speak to people: no pushing to deposit more, trade more or chase losses.

d.text: Your honest test: would you be comfortable if each user read your messages after losing their deposit? If not, rewrite them.

steps.h: Worked example: a planning value for RevShare
steps.p: Example. Your past cohorts suggest about $60 of RevShare per FTD over 12 months. Because RevShare is uncertain, cut it by 30% before planning. Your planning value per FTD is $42, which you treat as the payout.
steps.more: Example maths: $60 × 0.7 = $42. With a 25% margin, target CPA is $42 × 0.75 = $31.50, break-even is $42, the zero-conversion kill line is 2 × $31.50 = $63, and the CPA kill line after 3 × target spend ($94.50) is the lower of 1.5 × $31.50 = $47.25 and $42, which is $42. The 30% cut is our starting rule, not a law. Use a bigger cut until you have at least 3 months of your own cohort data for that geo.

$42 planning value
steps.say: Here's how to get a planning value for RevShare. Example: your past cohorts suggest about sixty dollars of RevShare per F T D over twelve months. Because RevShare is uncertain, cut it by thirty percent before planning. Sixty times zero point seven is forty two dollars, and you treat that as the payout. With a twenty five percent margin, your target C P A is thirty one fifty. The thirty percent cut is a starting rule, not a law. Use a bigger cut until you have at least three months of your own cohort data for that geo.

steps.h: Questions to ask before you accept
steps.p: Ask these in writing and keep the replies in your offer folder. A partner who cannot answer them clearly is telling you how a dispute would go later.
d: How is net revenue defined, and what is deducted?
Is there negative carryover, and does it ever reset?
How long is RevShare paid per client?
Can the deal be changed without notice, and does a change apply to existing clients?
What is the minimum payment threshold and the payment term?
Which events can you send as postbacks?

And which events can you receive as postbacks? Keep the replies in your offer folder. A partner who can't answer clearly is telling you how a dispute would go later.

steps.h: Common mistakes and the fix
steps.p: These mistakes often follow one good RevShare month or a manager's push to switch models. Decide models on your cash and your own cohort data, not on stories about other affiliates.

a.title: Mistake
items: Take RevShare with no cash buffer
Ignore negative carryover
Judge RevShare on one cohort
Assume 'lifetime' means forever

b.title: Fix
items: Start on CPA until you have data and cash
Model a losing month before you sign
Use a planning value with a 30% cut
Get the term per client in writing

steps.say: These mistakes often follow one good RevShare month, or a manager's push to switch models. On the left: taking RevShare with no cash buffer, ignoring negative carryover, judging RevShare on one cohort, and assuming lifetime means forever. On the right, the fixes: start on C P A until you have data and cash, model a losing month before you sign, use a planning value with a thirty percent cut, and get the term per client in writing. Decide on your cash and your own cohort data, not on stories about other affiliates.

steps.h: Starting decision rules for payout models
steps.p: Starting rules to adapt as your data grows. They keep you on the safer model until your own numbers, not a manager's forecast, justify more risk.
d: Start every new geo on CPA or hybrid, not pure RevShare
Consider RevShare only with 3+ months of cohort data and 3 months of spend in reserve
Planning value = expected RevShare per FTD × 0.7
Kill at 2 × target CPA spent with 0 qualified FTDs; kill if CPA > lower of 1.5 × target and break-even after 3 × target spend
Scale +20% every ≥ 48 hours when CPA ≤ 0.8 × target with ≥ 3 qualified FTDs
steps.say: Here are starting rules for payout models, to adapt as your data grows. Start every new geo on C P A or hybrid, not pure RevShare. Consider RevShare only with three or more months of cohort data and three months of spend in reserve. Planning value is expected RevShare per F T D times zero point seven. Kill at two times target C P A spent with zero qualified F T Ds, or if C P A is above the lower of one point five times target and break even after three times target spend. And scale twenty percent every forty eight hours or more, when C P A is at or below zero point eight times target with three or more qualified F T Ds.

lessons.title: The user journey: registration, KYC and FTD
objectives: By the end you can map every step from click to qualified FTD and measure the drop at each one.

steps.h: Why the money hides after registration
steps.p: Most beginners watch clicks and registrations because they arrive fast. Yet in trading, many registrations never deposit, often because of identity checks the broker must run by law. The gap between registration and qualified FTD is where most of your profit is won or lost.

d.b: A registration is not a client
d.s: Watch the steps between sign-up and deposit.

steps.say: Here's why this lesson matters. Most beginners watch clicks and registrations, because they arrive fast. steps.h: What KYC checks and why
steps.p: Know Your Customer checks are part of anti-money-laundering law in most countries. Brokers must confirm who the client is before they can trade or withdraw. The exact checks depend on the regulator and the entity, so ask your broker what users in your geo will see.
d: Identity|Passport, national ID or driving licence
Address|Utility bill or bank statement, often recent
Liveness|A selfie or short video to match the ID
Appropriateness|Questions on trading knowledge in some regions
Source of funds|For larger deposits or on request
Sanctions and age|Screening, and adults only
steps.say: K Y C means know your customer. These checks are part of anti money laundering law in most countries. Brokers must confirm who the client is before they can trade or withdraw. Look at the cards. Identity, with a passport, national I D or driving licence. Address, with a utility bill or bank statement. Liveness, a selfie or short video to match the I D. Appropriateness questions in some regions. Source of funds for larger deposits. And sanctions and age screening, adults only. The exact checks depend on the regulator, so ask your broker what users in your geo will see.

Revenue is fourteen seventy, profit two seventy, a margin of about eighteen percent, much thinner. Your rules must use the number you're actually paid on.

steps.h: Worked example: the value of honest preparation
steps.p: Example. You add a clear line to your lander: 'You will need a valid ID and proof of address.' KYC submission rises from 60% to 70% of registrations while the later rates stay the same. Qualified FTDs rise from 21 to 24.5 on the same spend.

steps.h: Honest fixes versus harmful fixes
steps.p: Some ways of lifting KYC completion are fraud or put users at risk. The honest ways all work by setting expectations and helping real, eligible adults finish a legal check, never by getting around it.

a.title: Never do this
items: Hide that ID is required
Give answers to the appropriateness test
Collect or forward users' documents yourself
Let anyone use another person's ID

b.title: Do this
items: Say ID is needed before sign-up
List documents and photo tips
Point users to the broker's own support
Invite people to stay on demo if unsure

steps.say: Compare honest fixes with harmful ones. On the left, never do this: hide that I D is required, give answers to the appropriateness test, collect or forward users' documents yourself, or let anyone use another person's I D. Some of those are fraud, and they put users at risk. On the right, do this: say I D is needed before sign up, list documents and photo tips, point users to the broker's own support, and invite people to stay on demo if they're unsure.

steps.h: The terms in a qualification rule
steps.p: Read every word of the rule on the offer page and confirm it in writing. Small details, such as whether the deposit is counted in total or in one payment, change who counts.
d: Baseline or raw FTD|Any first deposit at all
Minimum deposit|e.g. at least $100, single or cumulative
Activity rule|e.g. 0.5 lots or 5 trades
Window|Must happen within e.g. 30 days of sign-up
Exclusions|Duplicates, bonus-only, some payment methods
Geo rule|Only users from approved countries count
steps.say: Here are the terms in a qualification rule. A baseline or raw F T D is any first deposit at all. A minimum deposit, for example at least a hundred dollars, single or cumulative. An activity rule, like half a lot or five trades. A window, for example within thirty days of sign up. Exclusions, like duplicates, bonus only, or some payment methods. And a geo rule, so only users from approved countries count. Read every word on the offer page and confirm it in writing, because small details change who counts.

steps.h: What a lot is
steps.p: Activity rules are often in lots. In forex, one standard lot is 100,000 units of the base currency. A mini lot is 0.1 and a micro lot is 0.01. Fifty micro-lot trades add up to half a standard lot.
steps.more: Lot sizes for gold, indices, shares and crypto CFDs are defined differently by each broker, so 0.5 lots on gold is not the same exposure as 0.5 lots on EUR/USD. Ask the network how the rule is counted for each instrument. Never encourage users to trade more to meet an activity rule. If users only qualify because someone pushed them to trade, the deal is harming them and the broker may reverse the payout.

Check the platform's current financial and crypto policies, the law in your users' country, and the broker's licence for that country before you run. This is education, not legal or financial advice.

d: Go only if the licence gate passes and no fixed-expiry products reach your users
Budget per ad set = 3 × target per raw FTD

quiz.q: Offer A pays $150 with 40% qualifying. Offer B pays $90 with 75% qualifying. Which pays more per raw FTD?
The manager cannot name the licensed entity for your geo but offers a higher payout. What does the scorecard say?
options: The licence is a gate, so the offer is out
Ask users which entity they used
quiz.why: The licence line is a gate. If it fails, no other number matters.

quiz.q: Target per raw FTD is $30. What is the test budget for 3 ad sets at 3 × target?
quiz.why: 3 × $30 = $90 per ad set; × 3 ad sets = $270.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest red flag?
options: A manager suggesting you tell users they can earn daily
quiz.why: Income claims are banned and misleading; a partner pushing them is a serious warning sign.

quiz.q: An ad set has spent $95 with 4 qualified FTDs over 3 days. Target $30. What do the rules say?
quiz.why: CPA is $95 ÷ 4 = $23.75, which is below 0.8 × $30 = $24, with at least 3 qualified FTDs and 48+ hours, so scale +20%.

lessons.say_intro: A good funnel on the wrong offer still loses. In this lesson you'll learn to read a trading offer page for the eight facts that decide its value, compare offers on effective payout, score them, ask a manager the right questions in writing, and plan your first test budget with exact rules.
lessons.say_outro: So, choose the offer with numbers, not the headline: gate on the licence, compare effective payout, get answers in writing, and test one offer with clear kill and scale rules. Your task: shortlist two trading offers for one geo, fill the scorecard for both, send the manager your questions in writing, and calculate the test budget for the one you choose. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: You spent $120 on an ad set. Network shows 0 qualified FTDs. Target per raw FTD is $55 and the postback works. What do you do?
options: Kill: spend is above 2 × target with 0 conversions
exam.why: 2 × $55 = $110. $120 with 0 conversions passes the zero-conversion kill line.

exam.q: Offer pays $90 per qualified FTD. Your qualification rate is 60% and you want a 25% margin. What is your target per raw FTD?
A network offers 'digital trading' with 2-minute trades that pay 88% if right. The payout is double your current offer. What do you do?
options: Test it with a small budget
Run it under a different name
Decline: it works as a binary option, which major ad platforms prohibit
exam.why: Fixed expiry and fixed payout make it a binary or digital option. Steer to licensed forex, CFD or exchange offers.

exam.q: RevShare carryover is −$1,200. This month's net revenue is $2,000 on 25% RevShare. What are you paid?
An ad set has spent $150 over 4 days with 4 qualified FTDs. Target is $45. What do you do?
options: Keep: CPA $37.50 is below target but above 0.8 × target ($36)
exam.why: $150 ÷ 4 = $37.50. It is under target but not at or below $36, so keep without scaling.

exam.q: 200 registrations, 50% submit KYC, 75% of those are approved, 30% of approved deposit. How many FTDs?
Expected RevShare is $100 per FTD. Using the 30% cut, what is your break-even for planning?
exam.why: $100 × 0.7 = $70 planning value, which is your break-even.

exam.q: You spend $60 a day and the first payment arrives 40 days after you start. How much cash must you fund first?
exam.why: $60 × 40 = $2,400 of spend before the first payment.

exam.q: A user in your Telegram bot asks how to answer the broker's trading knowledge test. What do you do?
options: Send the answers so they qualify
Tell them it checks whether the product suits them, answer honestly, and suggest a demo first
exam.why: The appropriateness test protects users. Coaching around it harms people and can be fraud.

exam.q: Which deal term should you get in writing before accepting a RevShare deal?
options: The colour of the tracking link
How net revenue is defined and whether carryover applies
exam.why: Net revenue definition and carryover decide what you are actually paid.
